opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The gap was striking once you looked at it. Most of the world's valuable enterprise data sits in relational databases: customers, transactions, products, events, all spread across many tables linked by primary and foreign keys. Yet machine learning benchmarks had largely ignored that. We had great benchmarks for images, text, and single flat tables, but almost nothing that captured real multi-table relational structure.

So in practice, when someone wants to predict customer churn or what a user will buy next, the standard workflow is that a data scientist manually joins tables, aggregates, and hand-engineers features into one big flat table, then trains something like gradient boosted trees on it. That process is slow, error-prone, and throws away much of the relational signal. The research community didn't have a principled way to ask whether we could learn directly on the database end to end, the way deep learning replaced hand-crafted features in vision and language.

RelBench was our attempt to fill that gap. We collected real relational databases from different domains, like e-commerce, social Q&A, sports, and clinical data, and defined realistic predictive tasks on them: entity-level classification and regression, and recommendation-style link prediction. We were careful about time. Everything is split temporally, so you're always predicting the future from the past, which avoids the leakage that makes many benchmarks look easier than real deployments.

Alongside the benchmark we proposed relational deep learning, where you treat the database as a heterogeneous temporal graph, with rows as nodes and key relationships as edges, and apply graph neural networks directly. A key part of the work was a user study comparing this to experienced data scientists doing manual feature engineering. The learned models matched or beat the human pipelines on many tasks while needing a small fraction of the human effort. That was the real point: give the community a standard, realistic testbed so we can make measurable progress on learning from relational data, which is where so much real-world value lives.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts flat-table benchmarks with relational data, but does not explain that benchmark creators release single-table data because prevailing machine-learning practice assumes single-table input.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks covered single flat tables but had “almost nothing” capturing real multi-table relational structure.

r003.rationale: The response discusses manual feature engineering in data-science workflows, but does not say typical single-table Kaggle competitions provide already-engineered features to participants.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. So the motivation for RelBench really came from looking at where the data actually lives inside organizations. If you walk into basically any company, the most valuable data they have is sitting in a relational database: a set of tables linked by primary and foreign keys. Customers, transactions, products, events, and so on. That's the substrate on which most real predictive tasks are defined, things like churn, lifetime value, fraud, demand forecasting.

And yet, if you look at the machine learning benchmark landscape, almost none of it reflects that. We have fantastic benchmarks for images, for text, for single-table tabular data, for graphs in isolation. But the standard way people do machine learning on relational data is still, honestly, manual feature engineering. A data scientist writes a bunch of SQL joins and aggregations to flatten the tables into one big feature matrix, and then trains gradient boosted trees on top of it. That process is slow, it's brittle, it depends enormously on the skill and intuition of whoever wrote the queries, and critically, it throws away most of the structure in the data.

So the gap we wanted to address was twofold. First, there was simply no shared, realistic benchmark for predictive tasks over multi-table relational databases, with proper temporal splits so you don't leak the future into training. Second, we wanted to make the case that deep learning can work directly on the relational structure, end to end, without someone hand-crafting features. The idea is that a relational database is naturally a graph: rows are nodes, foreign keys are edges. Once you see it that way, graph neural networks become a very natural tool, and you can learn the representations rather than engineer them.

RelBench is our attempt to give the community a standard place to test that hypothesis. We pulled together a diverse set of real databases across different domains, defined a range of node-level and link-level prediction tasks on them, and set things up so that you can compare a learned relational model head to head against the feature engineering baseline that practitioners actually use today. And what we found, which was encouraging, is that the learned approach can match or beat the expert-engineered pipelines while cutting the human effort dramatically. Our hope is that this becomes the kind of catalyst for relational deep learning that ImageNet was for computer vision.

r001.rationale: The response says standard practice flattens relational data into a single feature matrix, but does not explain that benchmark creators release single-table data because prevailing practice assumes single-table inputs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts abundant single-table benchmarks with the lack of shared, realistic benchmarks for predictive tasks over multi-table relational databases.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Kaggle competitions or that their supplied features are already engineered.

astra-6.text:
The gap we wanted to address is that so much real-world data lives in relational databases, but our machine learning benchmarks tend to assume that the data has already been turned into a single, clean table. In practice, getting to that table is a huge part of the work. You have customers, transactions, products, all in different tables, and someone has to decide how to join them and what features to compute.

With RelBench, we wanted to benchmark learning directly from that relational structure. We provide databases and predictive tasks, so the challenge is to use information across connected tables to make a prediction. And we pay particular attention to time: if you’re predicting a future outcome, you should only have access to information that was available at the time of the prediction.

The goal is to make this setting accessible and reproducible, so we can measure progress toward models that learn from relational data with less manual feature engineering.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks tend to assume real-world data has already been turned into a single clean table, which conveys the single-table-input assumption behind the benchmark gap.

r002.rationale: It does not state that multi-table benchmarks are scarce relative to single-table benchmarks.

r003.rationale: It mentions the work of joining tables and computing features, but does not identify Kaggle competitions or say they supply participants with already-engineered features.

sol-6.1.text:
The gap we wanted to address is that so much enterprise data lives in relational databases, but our machine learning benchmarks usually start with a single, already prepared table. That leaves out a big part of the real problem: how do you learn from information spread across multiple tables connected by primary and foreign keys?

With RelBench, we wanted to provide realistic relational databases together with well-defined prediction tasks and a consistent evaluation framework. For example, you might predict whether a customer will make a purchase, using their history and information about products and transactions. You also need to respect time, so the model only sees information that would have been available when the prediction was made.

The goal is to make it possible to compare approaches reproducibly and advance machine learning directly over relational data, rather than assuming someone has already done all the joins and feature engineering for you.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks usually start with a single prepared table, but does not explain that benchmark creators do so because prevailing ML practice assumes single-table input.

r002.rationale: It contrasts benchmarks that usually start with one table with the missing challenge of learning across related tables, identifying the lack of multi-table benchmarks as the gap.

r003.rationale: It mentions prepared tables and prior joins or feature engineering generally, but does not identify typical single-table Kaggle competitions as supplying engineered features to participants.
